overview: The exact atlas id “soomra-emirate” spans 1100 to 1200. Its decoded 35-position polygon is one coarse display shape, not a surveyed Soomra border or modern Sindh. It includes tested Mansura, Aror, Banbhore, Thatta, Sehwan, Sukkur, and Badin, yet excludes Umarkot, Mithi, Nagarparkar, Multan, Kutch, and Gujarat. Historical Soomra or Sumra power belonged chiefly to Lower Sindh and continued beyond this map window, but its beginnings, rulers, genealogy, capitals, and reach survive through conflicting later chronicles, regional reconstructions, archaeology, and oral tradition. The safest story therefore joins political uncertainty to well-bounded regional evidence: river cultivation, caravan routes, Indian Ocean exchange, clay and brick buildings, craft debris, waterworks, and objects from long-lived towns. Ports and channels changed as the Indus delta shifted; a site’s occupation does not make every find a government project. Merchants, rulers, and religious buildings are easier to see than most families, children, patients, or waste workers, so daily-life sections name those gaps. At 1200 every tested member point changes to the atlas’s Khwarazmian color. That is an editorial seam, not a dated Soomra collapse, conquest, or population replacement.

periods.title: 1100 to 1107: the atlas begins; one reconstruction names Sanghar
periods.summary: The atlas first draws its Soomra feature in 1100. A University of Karachi-hosted reconstruction assigns Sanghar a reign from 1092 to 1107, already crossing the software boundary. The dates are an attributed proposal, not a securely contemporary king list or proof of the polygon’s extent.

periods.title: 1107 to 1120: a disputed early succession
periods.summary: A major historical compilation warns that Soomra lineage, ruler sequence, duration, and reach are exceptionally difficult because surviving narratives are late and inconsistent. The teaching period therefore marks an uncertain early succession rather than naming a precise transfer of power that the surviving evidence cannot securely date.

periods.title: 1120 to 1135: later lists refuse to align
periods.summary: Sindhi Language Authority-hosted historical discussion preserves contradictory names, successions, and dates. That disagreement is itself evidence about the archive: later writers remembered Soomra rule, but they did not leave one dependable year-by-year record. No single list is promoted into an official atlas chronology here.

periods.title: 1135 to 1142: proposed centers remain archaeological questions
periods.summary: Regional reconstructions associate early Soomra authority with lower-Sind centers, including Tharri, but identification and dating vary. The site has not yielded the kind of excavation record needed to turn a capital tradition into a street-level portrait. This phase therefore keeps court geography explicitly provisional.

periods.title: 1142 to 1154: one reconstruction begins Umar I
periods.summary: The University of Karachi-hosted sequence assigns Umar I a reign beginning in 1142 and lasting to 1181. It is useful for teaching one regional reconstruction, but not for declaring a universally accepted sovereign. Settlement, trade, and household evidence are dated independently wherever possible.

periods.title: 1154 to 1165: al-Idrisi describes towns from Sicily
periods.summary: Al-Idrisi completed his Arabic world geography for the Norman court in Sicily around 1154. His compilation describes Debal and Mansura, including buildings, foods, markets, shipping, and imported goods. It is near-contemporary learned geography, not a local census or eyewitness diary from every place.

periods.title: 1165 to 1175: river channels and coastlines keep moving
periods.summary: Historical geography shows the Indus delta and Rann changing through silting and shifting channels. These processes redirected cultivation, pasture, landing places, and routes without waiting for a ruler’s reign to end. A port’s fortunes could change because water moved as well as because armies did.

periods.title: 1175 to 1182: Ghurid pressure reaches the Indus
periods.summary: Encyclopaedia Iranica dates Ghurid operations against Multan and Uch to 1175. Multan lies outside the atlas polygon, so the event belongs to the wider political setting rather than an automatic claim of occupation everywhere inside the colored shape. Lower-Sind communities still faced a changing military horizon.

periods.title: 1182 to 1195: local rule under acknowledged suzerainty
periods.summary: Iranica reports that Sumeras in Lower Sind acknowledged Ghurid suzerainty in 1182. That wording permits continuing local authority beneath an external claim; it does not prove uniform administration, taxation, or garrisons throughout the atlas shape. Political hierarchy and everyday government could operate on different scales.

periods.title: 1195 to 1200: dynastic continuity crosses the atlas seam
periods.summary: Bosworth’s dynastic manual carries Soomra rule beyond 1200. At the endpoint the atlas nevertheless recolors every tested member point. Neither the manual nor the map supplies a Soomra fall in that year, so this final teaching period closes with political and social continuity rather than an invented collapse.

sections.title: Read the map before trusting the name

items.text: The exact live id is “soomra-emirate,” named “Soomra Emirate,” with approximate dates 1100 to 1200. It occurs in one border file and still lacks a researched card, accepted override, or completed identity review. Its imported dynasty summary is a starting clue, not finished medieval geography.

The 1100 feature is one Polygon with one ring and 35 decoded positions. Its bbox is 63.60003600036001, 23.675716060759996 to 71.4049140491405, 32.53184889897436; decoded geometry SHA-256 is 6923b4ad863a03c06c5de04536f03cac8303026506ef9a1cb1a6311b211d0ce5. These are reproducible atlas display-data facts, not surveyed medieval borders.

Tested Mansura, Aror, Banbhore, Thatta, Karachi, Hyderabad, Sehwan, Larkana, Sukkur, Mirpur Khas, and Badin lie inside the polygon. Umarkot, Mithi, Nagarparkar, Multan, Lahore, Kutch, central Rann, Gujarat, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Quetta, Turbat, and Kandahar lie outside. The shape cannot stand for all places called Sindh.

At 1000, every future-member probe belongs to the atlas’s Buyid Emirate layer; at 1100, all eleven enter “soomra-emirate”; at 1200, all move to “khwarazmian-dynasty.” These synchronized software switches are editorial regimes. They do not show eleven communities changing rulers, language, or identity on New Year’s Day.

The target directly shares encoded arcs in 1100 with “ghaznavid-emirate,” “seljuk-empire,” “hindu-kingdoms-1100,” and “solankis.” By 1279, every tested former member probe falls in the Delhi Sultanate layer. Arc contact and later recoloring describe this dataset’s topology, not diplomatic treaties or a single historical successor chain.

sections.title: Rulers, capitals, and power with uncertainty attached

items.text: A foundational difficulty is documentary: the historical compilation behind this discussion says Soomra origin, genealogy, ruler order, duration, and extent are hard to determine from late and inconsistent accounts. It also cautions that their authority was neither extensive nor absolute. This card therefore avoids a confident palace-to-palace narrative.

The University of Karachi-hosted study offers a usable but explicitly reconstructive sequence: Sanghar to 1107, Khafif II to 1142, Umar I to 1181, Dodo III to 1195, and Bhoongar II afterward. Those dates organize teaching periods; they are not presented as contemporary annals or universally accepted reigns.

A Sindhi Language Authority-hosted account preserves alternative names and successions that do not align neatly with other lists. Rather than “fix” the contradictions by choosing whichever date fits the map, the card treats them as evidence of later memory and the thinness of securely dated political documentation.

Regional historical maps associate Soomra power with Lower Sindh and propose centers such as Tharri, but a colored reconstruction cannot by itself establish court residence, administrative reach, or continuous occupation. Capital labels here remain attributed hypotheses, and the atlas polygon is never treated as a matching tax district.

In 1182, according to Encyclopaedia Iranica, Sumeras in Lower Sind acknowledged Ghurid suzerainty. Acknowledgment can coexist with local rulers and institutions; it is not evidence that Ghurid officials suddenly governed each village. The bounded claim is a changed political relationship during continuing regional Soomra authority.

sections.title: River farming, ports, markets, and Indian Ocean links

items.text: Al-Idrisi’s c.1154 compilation calls Debal a populous ship station whose merchants stored goods in bulk. It lists commodities arriving from Oman, China, and India. This is strong evidence for an Indian Ocean commercial node, but written Debal should not be silently equated with every archaeological layer at Banbhore.

The Government of Sindh places Banbhore’s fortified settlement beside an old Indus channel near the coast and records a long occupation sequence. That setting explains why river and sea routes mattered. The official page treats identification with Debal as a proposal, so the card keeps text and site evidence distinct.

Banbhore excavators report both locally made materials and imports from Iran, alongside thousands of worked ivory, bone, and shell fragments. Ports were workplaces as well as exchange points: sailors, brokers, carriers, guards, craftspeople, and food sellers all made trade possible, though most remain unnamed in elite texts.

A UNESCO comparative dossier dates Banbhore’s exchange and occupation sequence into the thirteenth century. That matters because another institutional summary emphasizes decline in the eleventh. Different archaeological syntheses therefore resist a tidy “port closes” date; activity, routes, and neighborhoods may have contracted or shifted unevenly.

The Indus carried fertile silt and commercial traffic, but its channels migrated. Historical geography describes delta silting and the Rann’s transformation toward salt marsh. Farmers, fishers, pastoralists, and boat crews had to adjust to water moving under them; rulers could command people more easily than command a river.

sections.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work

items.text: Al-Idrisi describes Debal houses built of clay and wood and Mansura buildings of brick, tile, and plaster. These compact urban sketches show locally available materials and different building traditions. They do not describe every rural hut, mobile camp, elite residence, or repair crew across the enormous polygon.

Banbhore’s museum inventory includes storage jars, glass, glazed wares, and Chinese pottery across broad medieval phases. Jars point toward storing water, grain, oil, or other goods, while imported ceramics mark exchange. Without a sealed 1100 to 1200 household context, no object becomes a typical Soomra kitchen utensil.

A 1981 Mansura field diary indexes wheat, animal and bird bones, a cooking furnace, storage jar, copper bowl, weights, bangles, and structural phases. These finds illuminate food preparation and household labor at the site, but an excavation index cannot assign every item to this exact century or one social group.

The 1982 diary adds fish bones, cock bones, eggshell, date-palm material, fireplaces, grinding equipment, and rubbish pits. The list is a vivid pantry with awkward paperwork: bones survive better than porridge, and indexed finds still need stratigraphic study before anyone declares a universal lunch menu.

Al-Idrisi reports Mansura’s people eating fish and meat, using dates and sugar, and obtaining several fruits; he also comments on clothing and coinage. His city description supports market variety, not equal access. Wealth, occupation, age, season, religion, and distance from town all shaped what people wore and ate.

sections.title: Families, social life, belief, and unequal voices

items.text: Mansura excavators recorded residential rooms, verandas, courtyards, partitions, and water fittings. These spaces hosted repeated domestic work and social life, probably by households, but walls cannot reveal whether residents formed nuclear, extended, servant-containing, or workshop families. Architecture supplies a stage; it does not hand us the cast list.

The 1966 Mansura diary indexes shell and glass bangles, beads, rings, decorated pieces, and household objects. Such belongings show adornment and personal choice. Automatically assigning each ornament to women, one religion, or one status group would replace evidence with expectation, so ownership and family meaning remain open.

Banbhore’s craft debris and imported wares reveal overlapping communities of makers, merchants, sailors, consumers, and laborers. Archaeology identifies activities more readily than names or kinship. Production zones might involve households, specialists, apprentices, or hired workers, but the surviving debris does not specify their family arrangements.

Mansura’s ruined neighborhoods, religious buildings, coins, jewelry, and everyday objects show a socially varied city whose occupation long predated and outlasted this map interval. The government summary does not sort finds into Soomra, non-Soomra, Muslim, Hindu, rich, poor, male, or female categories; this card refuses to do so for it.

Dodo and Chanesar became powerful figures in Sindhi oral tradition, but an academic study finds no documented version of their epic before the seventeenth century. The story matters as later social memory, performance, and moral debate. It cannot function as a twelfth-century transcript of marriage, family conflict, or court politics.

sections.title: Children, education, languages, and a written sample

items.text: The 1966 Mansura excavation index records children’s teeth, a toy rattle, a toy grinding mill, animal figurines, game objects, and small balls. These are rare openings onto childhood and learning by imitation or play. Mixed deposits prevent assigning every toy to one twelfth-century child, classroom, or family.

Medieval madrasas trained advanced students through teachers, texts, law, and religious learning, but the general Iranica account does not establish a named Soomra school. For most local children this packet has no enrollment list, timetable, or curriculum. Household, workshop, worship, and play-based learning remain likely but unmeasured contexts.

An academic article dates a named madrasa at Uch to 1206 to 1222, just after this card’s endpoint. It is useful precisely as a boundary: later evidence cannot be pulled backward to prove an institution in 1150. Children undoubtedly learned, but this packet cannot securely locate a period classroom.

Arabic served learned, religious, and commercial writing, while Sindhi and other regional speech traditions connected households and markets. A university course unit also describes earlier translation across Arabic and a local language. None of this supplies a standardized twelfth-century Sindhi schoolbook or proves that every resident read either script.

Written sample, c.1154, describing Debal: Arabic “ومدينة الديبل كثيرة الناس” (wa-madīnat al-Daybul kathīrat al-nās), “The city of Debal has many people.” The wording belongs to al-Idrisi’s Sicily-based Arabic geography, not a local inscription, school exercise, or sample of ordinary speech; manuscript spellings may vary.

sections.title: Medicine, health, diet, and honest absences

items.text: This source packet found no securely localized 1100 to 1200 physician’s kit, prescription, hospital, medical school, or named healer at the audited sites. That is an evidence gap, not proof that treatment vanished. Importing famous medicine from Baghdad would make a smoother story and a less honest card.

Inundation farming depended on timing, channel maintenance, and collective labor. A regional irrigation history reconstructs long-lived practices rather than measuring this century field by field. Reliable water supported food and health; floods, stagnant pools, salinity, or channel abandonment could threaten them. The mechanisms are sound, but exact acreage is unavailable.

Children’s teeth and animal bones from Mansura can support future study of age, diet, disease, and environment, but the 1966 diary is an excavation index rather than a published bioarchaeological diagnosis. A tooth proves a child was present more securely than it reveals what medicine that child received.

Fish, bird, and animal bones, eggshell, wheat, dates, and grinding equipment show varied foods at Mansura across its occupation. Variety does not equal nutritional equality. The 1982 diary offers no household ration tables, famine series, or disease statistics, and the broad layers cannot all be assigned to Soomra rule.

Cooking furnaces, storage jars, a copper bowl, and grain remains help reconstruct food safety and labor only indirectly. The 1981 diary does not record handwashing rules, contamination, or who ate first. It shows material practices; differences by wealth, gender, age, occupation, and neighborhood remain mostly beyond the surviving evidence.

sections.title: Water, waste, baths, and the toilet question

items.text: Archaeological synthesis describes Mansura residences with wells, sometimes using terracotta collars, and covered lined drains beneath or beside built space. Such systems required digging, lining, clearing, and repair. They demonstrate urban water engineering without proving pure water, equal household access, or a single citywide sewer authority.

Banbhore’s walled town used a lake or reservoir as a major water source, with access routes built into the settlement plan. Storage mattered at a dry coastal port, but reservoirs also collected silt and needed protection from waste. The archaeology does not preserve a neat medieval cleaning rota.

A 1977 to 1978 Mansura diary records water supply, a terracotta pipe, drains, rubbish, pits, ash, courtyards, and residential rooms. These features show the ordinary maintenance that kept neighborhoods usable. The index does not identify who carried water, swept waste, unclogged pipes, or controlled access.

The 1982 diary separately indexes a covered drain, terracotta soak pit, rubbish pits, streets, and household debris. Together they suggest more than one strategy for runoff and disposal. Because excavated features cross occupation phases, they cannot be advertised as a universal twelfth-century plumbing package with complimentary towels.

Near Banbhore’s mosque, channels may have served ablution and latrines; the archaeological interpretation is explicitly possible rather than certain. Baths are also reported elsewhere at the site. The responsible toilet answer is “some specialized facilities probably existed,” not that every home had a private bathroom or fragrant drains.

Banbhore’s plan includes heavy walls, bastions, gates, streets, religious space, housing, workshops, and water infrastructure. These works required designers, quarrying or brickmaking, transport, skilled masons, and repeated repair. A surviving wall is therefore evidence of organized labor, but not proof that the Soomra court commissioned every phase.

More than four thousand carved ivory, animal-bone, and shell fragments at Banbhore point to jewelry and furniture production. Waste flakes are a discovery about work, not just pretty objects: they reveal cutting, shaping, mistakes, and material supply. Dating remains site-specific and broader than a single ruler’s reign.

University of Bologna researchers use compositional study to distinguish Banbhore glass raw materials, production technologies, and possible connections with Middle Eastern and eastern industries. That method checks whether a shard was imported, copied, remelted, or locally made. Sparkle alone, charmingly, is not a shipping label.

A recent Banbhore synthesis records ivory and bone waste, glass, metallurgy, mother-of-pearl work, vessels, and imported porcelain across long sequences. The achievement lies in both production and redistribution. Individual finds cannot all be stamped “Soomra-made,” because occupation phases and trade networks cross political labels.

Museum displays preserve storage vessels, glazed pottery, glass, and Chinese ceramics from broad medieval phases. Some objects may overlap 1100 to 1200, yet display dates often span centuries. The safe discovery is sustained craft and exchange at the port, not a fictional inventory from one ruler’s dining room.

sections.title: Conflict, affected communities, and the 1200 seam

items.text: Ghurid campaigns reached Multan and Uch in 1175, followed by lower-Sind Sumeras acknowledging suzerainty in 1182. Warfare and political pressure affected provisions, transport animals, labor, taxes, and safety far beyond named rulers. The source does not map battles or garrisons onto every point inside the atlas polygon.

The Dodo-Chanesar epic remembers invasion, loyalty, betrayal, and communal suffering, but its documented versions are many centuries later. It should be taught as evolving oral memory rather than a battlefield dispatch. That distinction still leaves room to discuss how later communities understood the human costs of conflict.

Academic study finds no documented Dodo-Chanesar version before the seventeenth century, long after the events it narrates. Ruins and stories deserve attention, but matching a named wall, heroine, and exact twelfth-century event requires evidence the surviving epic record does not supply. Later memory remains valuable without becoming an eyewitness archive.

Bosworth’s dynastic manual carries Soomra rule beyond 1200. The exact ending varied by reconstruction and later traditions, so this card does not choose the atlas endpoint as a fall. Political relationships changed, but river communities, crafts, markets, languages, worship, and households continued through that artificial boundary.

At 1200 every tested member point becomes “khwarazmian-dynasty,” and by 1279 every one becomes “delhi-sultanate.” Banbhore’s comparative archaeological sequence also extends beyond 1200. Software colors, dynastic labels, and site occupation therefore run on different clocks; no mass disappearance or instant cultural replacement is inferred.

ending.text: At 1200 the exact “soomra-emirate” feature disappears and all eleven tested member points become the atlas’s “khwarazmian-dynasty” color; by 1279 they all sit in “delhi-sultanate.” Historical reconstructions continue Soomra rule beyond 1200, so the boundary is not a supported fall, conquest date, or population replacement. The override leaves fell null and names no single successor. River settlements, ports, farms, workshops, households, languages, religious communities, and water systems continued through the editorial seam.
